clue.text: Shelley records his "sneer of cold command"

definitions.text: Shelley records his "sneer of cold command"

parts.words: Shelley records his "sneer of cold command"
parts.note: Shelley's sonnet about a shattered statue in the desert describes the king's wrinkled lip and sneer of cold command; the clue asks for the sonnet's title and subject

explanation.surface: A poet writes down a tyrant's contemptuous expression.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted phrase comes from Shelley's 1818 sonnet, whose title is the Greek name of Pharaoh Rameses II.
explanation.definitionFit: The sonnet and the pharaoh it portrays share the one name, so the poem records the sneer of its own subject.

clue.text: While the water — sings " (John Dyer)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from the eighteenth-century Welsh poet John Dyer; the missing word is a gentle west wind

explanation.surface: A line of pastoral verse with a word left out for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: Quotation clues are a TLS staple: the solver must recall the poem, here John Dyer's landscape verse, where a soft breeze is said to sing.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word names a mild west wind, a stock figure of pastoral poetry.

clue.text: Monty had a part in his victory

definitions.text: Monty had a part in his victory

parts.words: Monty had a part in his victory
parts.note: turns round the title of a comic war memoir, Monty: His Part in My Victory, so 'his' is the memoir's author

explanation.surface: Field Marshal Montgomery helped someone win.
explanation.walkthrough: Spike Milligan, the comedian of The Goon Show, wrote a series of war memoirs including Monty: His Part in My Victory; the clue restates that title from the outside.
explanation.definitionFit: The comedian whose memoir title claims Montgomery contributed to the author's own victory.

clue.text: Rembrandt's security men

parts.note: Rembrandt's famous Amsterdam group portrait shows a civic militia company, the guardsmen of a town at night

explanation.surface: The guards employed by the Dutch painter.
explanation.walkthrough: The painting's popular English title also names the guards who patrol after dark.
explanation.definitionFit: The popular title of Rembrandt's militia painting also describes a body of guards on duty after dark.

clue.text: It will ever be the same, said Smart in the Hilliad

definitions.text: It will ever be the same, said Smart in the Hilliad

parts.words: It will ever be the same, said Smart in the Hilliad
parts.note: Christopher Smart's mock-heroic poem The Hilliad, attacking John Hill, has a line declaring this quality will ever be the same

explanation.surface: A remark about permanence attributed to the poet Christopher Smart.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the quality Smart's satire says never changes; the clue relies on the solver knowing The Hilliad (1753).
explanation.definitionFit: Emptiness of mind or silliness is the unchanging vice that Smart's satire mocks in its target.

clue.text: Writer for whom Peter øeg's physicist had a feeling

definitions.meaning: C. P. ..., English novelist and scientist, author of The Two Cultures

definitions.text: for whom Peter øeg's physicist had a feeling
definitions.meaning: Peter Høeg's novel Smilla's Feeling for ... names what its ice-expert heroine has a sense for

explanation.surface: A Danish novel's scientist was attracted to an author.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan drops the H of Høeg. The second definition rests on the English title of Høeg's novel about Smilla, a Greenlander expert in ice.
explanation.definitionFit: C. P. Snow was a novelist, and the novel title says Smilla has a feeling for frozen flakes.

clue.text: Rascal is revealed by her letters

definitions.text: Rascal is revealed by her letters

indicators.note: the letters of the first two words, rearranged, reveal the heroine's name

explanation.surface: A scoundrel is exposed through the correspondence a woman writes.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Richardson's novel is told in letters; its rake Lovelace, the rascal, is exposed by the heroine's correspondence. The letters of RASCAL IS rearrange to give her name.
explanation.definitionFit: Richardson's epistolary novel is named after the young woman whose letters tell the story of the rake who ruins her.

clue.text: Ornament of the church sounds impolite on panel

indicators.note: the word for impolite is said aloud to give a similar-sounding church word

parts.note: impolite means rude
a screen is a panel used to divide a space

explanation.surface: A church decoration seems rude when placed on a board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a link in a down clue: the homophone of RUDE sits on top of SCREEN. A rood is a crucifix, and the rood screen divides nave from chancel.
explanation.definitionFit: A carved partition beneath the crucifix, separating nave and chancel, is a decorative feature of a church.

clue.text: O'Neill confused by ornamental metalwork

indicators.note: confused means the letters of the name are muddled into a new order

explanation.surface: The playwright O'Neill is puzzled by decorative metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' asks for the letters of O'NEILL rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Niello is a black metallic inlay used to decorate engraved silver.

clue.text: The cardinal's was his for life

definitions.text: The cardinal's was his for life

parts.words: The cardinal's was his for life
parts.note: Cardinal Newman's autobiography is titled ... Pro Vita Sua, a defence of his own life; 'his for life' translates pro vita sua

explanation.surface: A cardinal held something for his whole lifetime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for life' looks like 'lifelong', but it renders the Latin pro vita sua from Newman's 1864 title.
explanation.definitionFit: Newman's book is a written defence of his life, which is what the Latin title word means.

clue.text: Provenance of Dvorak's Fifth

parts.note: Dvorak's symphony From the ... was numbered fifth on first publication (now the Ninth), and its title says where it came from

explanation.surface: Asking where a Czech composer's symphony originated.
explanation.walkthrough: The symphony now called No 9 was first published as No 5; its title says it comes from America.
explanation.definitionFit: The Americas, where Dvorak wrote the symphony, are what its subtitle names as its place of origin.

clue.text: One of Aristophanes' old jumpers

parts.note: Aristophanes wrote a comedy named after a chorus of croaking leaping amphibians; 'jumpers' are those creatures, not sweaters

explanation.surface: An old sweater belonging to the Greek playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jumpers' suggests the British word for sweaters, but it means leaping creatures, from the chorus of Aristophanes' comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: A single member of the croaking leaping chorus in Aristophanes' comedy.

clue.text: Shakespearean king might be a firstborn …

indicators.note: might be means the letters of the following phrase could be rearranged into the answer

explanation.surface: A royal character from Shakespeare could be an eldest son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' asks for the letters of A FIRSTBORN rearranged. Fortinbras, Prince of Norway, claims the Danish throne at the end of Hamlet.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norwegian prince who takes the Danish crown at the close of Hamlet.

clue.text: Accompaniment to royal progress warms cutie, anyhow

indicators.note: anyhow means in no particular order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something played as the monarch travels heats up a sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyhow' asks for the letters of WARMS and CUTIE rearranged. Handel's suite was written for George I's barge procession on the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: Handel composed the suite to be played on the Thames as King George I travelled by barge.

clue.text: … and wonder in English poetry seen by Swinburne's supporter as reborn

definitions.text: … and wonder in English poetry seen by Swinburne's supporter as reborn

parts.words: … and wonder in English poetry seen by Swinburne's supporter as reborn
parts.note: Theodore Watts-Dunton, who looked after Swinburne, wrote of The ... of Wonder in English Poetry, the word meaning rebirth

explanation.surface: A Victorian critic's view that poetic wonder came back to life.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links to 12-down, but the clue stands alone: Watts-Dunton, Swinburne's companion and protector, coined the phrase 'the Renascence of Wonder'.
explanation.definitionFit: A revival or rebirth, the word Watts-Dunton used for the return of wonder to poetry.

clue.text: "In pieces cut, the viper still did —" (Swift)

definitions.text: "In pieces cut, the viper still did —" (Swift)

parts.words: "In pieces cut, the viper still did —" (Swift)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Swift, drawing on the belief that a cut-up snake can join its pieces again

explanation.surface: A line of Swift's verse about a severed snake, with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing verb draws on the old belief that a severed snake could make itself whole again.
explanation.definitionFit: The cut pieces of the snake join back together, which the missing verb describes.

clue.text: Tune died sadly, and not changed

indicators.note: sadly here means badly, so the letters are put in a different order

explanation.surface: A melody faded mournfully and stayed the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' asks for the letters of TUNE and DIED rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A text left unedited has not been altered by an editor.

clue.text: Beckett's last plays? …

parts.note: Samuel Beckett's one-act play is named for the final stage of a chess game, where the last moves are played

explanation.surface: A question about the final dramas Beckett wrote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last plays' suggests Beckett's final works, but it means the closing moves of a chess game, which give the play its title.
explanation.definitionFit: The final phase of a chess game, the closing moves, gives Beckett's play its title.

clue.text: Lively chap in spirited dance

definitions.meaning: an archaic word for a gallant, high-spirited man
a lively Renaissance court dance in triple time

explanation.surface: An energetic man taking part in a vigorous dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link between the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: The word once meant a gay, valiant fellow and also names a brisk Tudor court dance.

clue.text: Devious movers from Dallas

parts.note: chess pieces whose L-shaped move is indirect; Dallas, read as a source, supplies the title meaning

explanation.surface: Sneaky removal men from Texas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'movers' suggests removal men, but it means chess pieces, whose L-shaped jump is the most roundabout move on the board.
explanation.definitionFit: The chess pieces that jump in an L shape move indirectly, so they are the devious ones.

clue.text: … and spoken words he poisoned, sadly

indicators.note: sadly here means in a sorry state, so the letters are put in a different order

explanation.surface: Words uttered by a man who regrettably used poison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' asks for the letters of HE and POISONED rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideophones are words that evoke a sound or sensation vividly, as in speech, such as 'zigzag'.

clue.text: Like Alasdair Gray's spare stories

parts.note: ... Tales (1985), a collection by Alasdair Gray with James Kelman and Agnes Owens; 'spare' means thin or sparse

explanation.surface: Describing the economical short fiction of a Scottish author.
explanation.walkthrough: Alasdair Gray was a Glasgow novelist; his shared collection with Kelman and Owens was called Lean Tales.
explanation.definitionFit: Spare and thin in style, the word that titled Gray's shared collection of short fiction.

clue.text: Some Spenserian enamel on the French armour

parts.note: au is French for 'to the' or 'at the'
mail is chain armour

explanation.surface: A Spenser text's decoration sits on French armour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is only a link: in a down clue the first piece sits on top of the second. The word is an archaic form of 'enamel' found in Spenser's Faerie Queene.
explanation.definitionFit: Spenser used this old form for enamelling or enamel work in The Faerie Queene.

clue.text: He saw it through

parts.note: H. G. Wells's novel Mr ... Sees It Through (1916) is about an Englishman enduring the First World War

explanation.surface: Someone persevered to the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue puts the title of Wells's wartime novel into the past tense, with its hero as 'He'.
explanation.definitionFit: The hero of Wells's novel is the man who sees the war through.

clue.text: Russian prince with no right to stiffness

indicators.note: with no means a letter is taken away from the word for stiffness

parts.note: rigor is stiffness, as in rigor mortis

explanation.surface: A Russian nobleman lacking the authority to be rigid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no' removes R from RIGOR. Prince Igor is the hero of Borodin's opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Borodin's opera is named after the medieval Russian prince who fought the Polovtsians.

clue.text: Australian novelist's dynasty leads and follows artist

indicators.note: leads and follows means the dynasty both comes before and after the artist

parts.note: the Han dynasty ruled China
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist
the same dynasty, used again

explanation.surface: An Australian writer's family line precedes and follows a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leads and follows' means the one dynasty stands both before and after the artist. Barbara Hanrahan was an Australian novelist and printmaker; the 's stands for 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: Barbara Hanrahan wrote novels such as The Scent of Eucalyptus set in Australia.

clue.text: Where Othello stabbed a malignant Turk

definitions.text: Where Othello stabbed a malignant Turk

parts.words: Where Othello stabbed a malignant Turk
parts.note: in his final speech Othello recalls that in a Syrian city he once smote a malignant and a turbaned Turk

explanation.surface: Asking the location of a Moorish general's attack.
explanation.walkthrough: Othello's last speech tells how 'in Aleppo once' he killed a Turk who beat a Venetian; he then stabs himself as he did that Turk.
explanation.definitionFit: The Syrian city Othello names in his dying speech as the scene of the stabbing.

clue.text: "The finest Elphberg of them all"

parts.note: in Anthony Hope's The Prisoner of Zenda the Englishman Rudolf, related to Ruritania's royal Elphberg family, is hailed as its best member

explanation.surface: Praise for the noblest member of a royal house.
explanation.walkthrough: Rudolf, the English hero of The Prisoner of Zenda, impersonates his cousin the King of Ruritania, and is called the finest of the Elphberg line.
explanation.definitionFit: The Englishman of Elphberg blood in Hope's novel is praised as the best of that royal family.
